objectives: Students will identify movements and persons prominent in the development of design of the built environment and their major contributions to the development of the profession of landscape architecture.
Students will identify significant works of contributors within specified time frames.
Students will describe and compare various styles or historic periods of design activity and the guiding concepts or design principles that characterized them.
Students will identify the physical resource conditions and the social, cultural and economic conditions that shaped the designs.
Students will define various concepts, principles, techniques or features constituting an introductory vocabulary for design.
topics: Introduction
Ancient Period - Egyptian, Persian, Mesopotamian, Greek and Roman gardens
Medieval Period - Christian European monastic and castle gardens, urban spaces
Islamic Spanish and Middle Eastern gardens
Italian Renaissance, Mannerist and Baroque gardens
French Renaissance chateaux gardens
French Baroque chateaux gardens and urban forms
English Tudor and Jacobean gardens
Romantic estate gardens and parks, urban spaces and parks
American Colonial - towns and gardens
American National - 19th-century town planning, civic design, public works, institutions, estate gardens
The creation of "Landscape Architecture"
Twentieth-century American Modernism in Landscape Architecture
Post-Modern landscape architecture

objectives: Students will be able to explain landscapes as complex artifacts and systems involving natural processes and human activities.
Students will be able to explain the systems approach to landscape management.
Students will be able to illustrate how adaptive management can be used to learn about structure, function, and change in the landscape over time.
Students will be able to assess significance and integrity of cultural landscapes.
Students will be able to apply principles of sustainability and resilience thinking to a cultural landscape management plan.
Students will have an appreciation of landscapes as complex artifacts involving natural processes and human activities.
Students will have an understanding of the rubric of preservation based on the concept of integrity and its application to landscapes and the field of landscape management.
Students will have an understanding of the systems approach to landscape management and how it can be used to address change over time.
topics: Introduction:
Landscape types and their management issues:
Landscape management vocabulary.
Landscape prototypes and their management issues.
Historic landscape preservation, the rubric of historic preservation and its
application to cultural landscapes.
The concept of integrity as applied to landscapes.
Cultural landscape reports.
Secretary of the Interior's standards for cultural landscapes.
Use issues.
Project:
A discussion paper exploring management issues for one landscape type of your choice.
A systems approach to managing landscapes:
Change in landscapes.

objectives: Students will critically compare and the contrast the fundamental assumptions and contributions of the main schools of thought that have influenced the design and development of cities and regions in the modern era.
Students will critically assess the merits and limitations of the major theoretical schools of thoughts in urban and environmental design.
Students will critically and selectively apply the history and theory behind the ideas discussed in the class to the design and development of communities today.
Students will make informed choices about which theories would be useful in their own doctoral research.
Students will develop the capacity to pose an answerable question that could be used as the main research question of their future dissertations.
Students will produce and present a paper related to the topic of their future dissertations while building on the theories and histories explored in the class.
topics: 1) Exploring the foundational questions: Why get a Ph.D.?
What is a theory?
What is history?
What is design?
What is the relationship between theory, history, and practice?
2) Exploring seminal readings in theory and history; analyzing major design theories with global impact.
3) Exploring how research questions are posed and answered in theory/history presentations.
4) Finding YOUR question and trying to answer it through student presentations and papers.
The course provides a critical perspective of the main theoretical foundations, the history of our disciplines, and the
It continues with exploring the role that history and theory play in the design of our built environments - and by the w
Is design derived from an individual agency (and which agency - professionals, practitioners, citizens?), or is it inesc
Is the history/theory of design simply the history/theory of the social world?
What is the relationship between history/theory and practice?
Is all practice based on theory/history?

objectives: Students will perform a critical analysis of topics in environmental design and planning fields.
Students will participate in discourse with peer Ph.D. students and faculty on relevant issues pertaining to doctoral studies in environmental design and planning.
Students will develop a culture of advanced academic inquiry amongst Ph.D. student cohorts.

Students will acquire breadth of knowledge of scholarly research in environmental design and planning through collaboration with students and faculty across the Ph.D. curriculum in the College of Environment and Design.
